pos: n. (the seventh son of Nahor by Milcah, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Yidlaph, he weepeth, or he droppeth, from dalaph, to drop, to drip, or to melt away in tears; named once, Genesis 22:22.
biblical_def: Jidlaph is the seventh of the eight sons borne to Nahor by Milcah, and he is named in a single line of a single verse: “And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel” (Genesis 22:22). Nothing else is recorded of him — no deed, no dwelling, no descendant. He is a name in a list, and the list is the point. The notice comes immediately after the binding of Isaac, and it comes as news carried to Abraham: “And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor” (Genesis 22:20). Abraham had just been given his son back from the altar; now he is told that his brother's house in Mesopotamia is multiplying. The register exists to reach the last name in it: “And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother” (Genesis 22:23). Jidlaph is one of the seven brothers God passed over on the way to the bride of Isaac. The LORD was arranging a marriage two chapters before the servant was sent, and He did it by giving a man eight sons in a far country. Jidlaph never knew he was in the story.

corruption_summary: Genealogies are dismissed as filler; Genesis 22 shows a list of forgotten names doing the quiet work of providence toward a marriage God had already appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader skips the lists, and the historical-critical handling of them goes further: it treats such registers as late tribal etiology rather than record. Scripture treats them as record, and as record with a purpose. The eight names of Genesis 22:22-23 are not decoration around Rebekah; they are the evidence that God had been building a household in Haran all the while Abraham was walking to Moriah. The chapter that shows the father of the faithful raising the knife ends by showing the LORD quietly stocking a well in Mesopotamia with the girl who would carry the promise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence works through the unrecorded. Seven of Milcah's eight sons contribute nothing to the narrative except the fact of their existence, and that fact establishes the eighth. A believer whose life leaves no line in any chronicle is not therefore outside the work; he may be the seventh name in a verse that exists to reach the eighth.

pos: n. (the sixth son of Nahor by Milcah, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Pildash, of uncertain sense; taken by the older lexicographers as flame of fire, or a steely weapon; named once, Genesis 22:22.
biblical_def: Pildash stands sixth in the register of Nahor's sons by Milcah: “And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel” (Genesis 22:22). Like his brothers Chesed, Hazo, and Jidlaph, he is named and no more. The eight sons are counted and closed in the next verse: “And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother” (Genesis 22:23). The placement of this short genealogy is deliberate. It follows the Angel of the LORD staying Abraham's hand on Mount Moriah, and it is delivered to Abraham as a report from home. The promise had just been reaffirmed in the strongest terms Scripture records: “That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven” (Genesis 22:17). Then the text turns to Haran and shows a brother's house filling with sons. Pildash is one of them. He is not a type, not a warning, not an example; he is a fact of the record, and the record is what the servant of Abraham will later depend upon when he asks the LORD for a sign at the well and finds Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor — Pildash's own niece.

corruption_summary: A name whose meaning is lost is treated as a sign the record is unreliable; Scripture is content to preserve a man's name without explaining it.
corruption_paragraphs: Pildash is one of a number of biblical names whose root cannot now be recovered with confidence. The historical-critical habit treats such opacity as a mark of legend. The opposite inference is the sound one: an inventor of genealogies supplies meanings, and a keeper of records does not. Scripture has preserved a man whose name it does not explain, in a list it does not expand, because the list is a record rather than a composition.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD knows names He has not explained to us. Pildash is unexplained in the text and fully known to God. The believer's comfort does not rest on being understood by the chroniclers, but on being written where it counts: “rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

pos: n. (a son of Nahor by his concubine Reumah, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Tachash, a badger, or the skin of some clean sea-creature used for the covering of the tabernacle; named once, Genesis 22:24.
biblical_def: Thahash is the third of the four sons borne to Nahor by his concubine: “And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she bare also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah” (Genesis 22:24). The verse is the last of the chapter, and it is the shadow cast by the eight sons of Milcah named just above it. Scripture does not commend Nahor's arrangement; it records it, as it records the concubines of Abraham and of Jacob's sons, with the consequences left to the narrative. The Authorized Version uses the same word for the covering of the tabernacle: “a covering above of badgers' skins” (Exodus 26:14), and the name Thahash is that word. A man was called Badger, and the hide of that creature was afterward laid over the dwelling-place of God — the outermost, plainest layer, the one that took the weather. Of the man himself nothing further is written. He fathered no tribe the record follows, and his line is not traced. He belongs to the set of names Scripture preserves without comment: real, numbered, and silent. The line of promise ran through Milcah's eighth son, not through Reumah's third.

corruption_summary: Concubinage in the patriarchal narratives is read as Scripture's endorsement; the text records the practice and lets its fruit be seen in whose line the promise did not run.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings press on a verse like this one. The first is the progressive claim that because Scripture reports concubinage without a rebuke attached, Scripture approves it, and therefore biblical sexual ethics are negotiable. The second is the older liberal claim that such notices are tribal fiction. Both fail on the text. Genesis narrates Nahor's concubine in the same breath that it closes the account of Milcah's eight sons, and the chapter that follows traces Rebekah — Milcah's granddaughter. The record is not neutral about outcomes even where it is silent about verdicts. One-man-one-woman marriage is the creation ordinance of Genesis 2:24, and every departure from it in the patriarchal narratives yields grief, rivalry, or a line that goes nowhere.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's silence is not consent. The Authorized Version names Reumah and her four sons, and never returns to them. A man may be truly recorded and still be outside the line of the covenant, and the way God kept His promise is read in whom He chose, not merely in whom He mentioned.

pos: n. (king of Zeboiim, one of the five kings of the vale of Siddim)
etymology: Hebrew Shem'eber, lofty flight, or soaring name, from shem, a name, and 'abar, to soar or to mount up; named once, Genesis 14:2.
biblical_def: Shemeber is king of Zeboiim, the fourth of the five kings of the plain who rebelled against Chedorlaomer: “That these made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar” (Genesis 14:2). He is named once, and he is named to be numbered among the defeated. The battle is joined in the next verses: “And there went out the king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (the same is Zoar;) and they joined battle with them in the vale of Siddim” (Genesis 14:8). Shemeber loses, and in losing he sets the stage for Abram's one recorded act of war — the rescue of Lot, the tithe to Melchizedek, and the refusal of Sodom's goods. His city will be destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah, and it is afterward named as a standing warning: “how shall I set thee as Zeboim?” (Hosea 11:8). A king whose name means soaring is named once, on the losing side, over a city that God would overthrow. Scripture records his title and nothing he did with it.

corruption_summary: The overthrow of the cities of the plain is recast as a myth about hospitality; Genesis names the kings, the coalition, the battlefield, and the year of the revolt.
corruption_paragraphs: The affirming reading of Sodom holds that the city fell for inhospitality rather than for the sin the prophets and apostles name. Scripture settles it without ambiguity: “Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire” (Jude 1:7). Zeboiim is one of those cities about them, and Shemeber was its king. The historical-critical reading goes the other way and treats Genesis 14 as late legend, yet the chapter is the most circumstantial war narrative in the patriarchal history — five kings named, four kings named, a thirteenth-year revolt, a named battlefield, a named spoil, and a named priest-king who received the tithe.

Shemeber's one verse is therefore worth more than it looks. It belongs to the record that establishes the cities of the plain as real places with real rulers, which is precisely what makes their overthrow a historical judgment rather than a cautionary tale. The principle to recover is that God's judgments fall on actual cities ruled by actual men, and that the LORD's long patience with them — the thirteen years, the rescue by Abram, the plea of Abraham — is no promise that judgment will not come.

pos: n. (father of Chalcol, Darda, Heman, and Ethan, the wise men Solomon surpassed)
etymology: Hebrew Machol, a dance, or the sound of dancing, from chul, to whirl or to dance; named once, 1 Kings 4:31.
biblical_def: Mahol is named once, and only as a father: “For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol: and his fame was in all nations round about” (1 Kings 4:31). The verse is a measurement. Solomon's wisdom is being weighed, and the weights chosen are the four wisest men the age could produce — and all four are Mahol's sons. Whatever house this was, it was the house that had the reputation for understanding, so that to say Solomon exceeded the sons of Mahol was to say he exceeded the summit of human learning. The gift itself was from God and had been asked for rightly: “And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore” (1 Kings 4:29). Mahol himself did nothing recorded. He is named because of his sons, as Jesse is named for David and Amram for Moses. A man whose name means a dance fathered the four great minds of his generation and is remembered in one clause as their father. The glory of the household went to the sons, and the honour of the verse went to the One who gave Solomon more.

corruption_summary: Wisdom is treated as a human attainment to be ranked; Scripture ranks it only to show that Solomon's came as a gift and was still not enough to keep him.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern handling of wisdom is comparative and self-referential: it measures insight against other insight and calls the top of the list enlightenment. First Kings does hold a comparison — Solomon against the sons of Mahol — but only to show the gift's source. God gave it, in answer to a prayer for an understanding heart rather than for riches or long life, and the nations came to hear it. The register of Mahol's four sons exists to mark a ceiling, and then to say that the ceiling was passed by a man who had asked God for the ability to govern.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the wisest man who ever reigned ended in idolatry, which settles whether natural wisdom can keep a soul. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 111:10) is the whole of the matter, and Solomon's own later writing is the proof by subtraction. Mahol's sons were the best the age had, Solomon surpassed them, and both together could not do what the fear of God does.

pos: n. (a son of Jehaleleel of the tribe of Judah, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Tirya, fear, or reverence; taken by some from yare', to fear; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:16.
biblical_def: Tiria is the third of the four sons of Jehaleleel in the genealogy of Judah: “And the sons of Jehaleleel; Ziph, and Ziphah, Tiria, and Asareel” (1 Chronicles 4:16). The verse stands in the long Judahite register that the Chronicler assembled after the captivity, when a returned remnant needed to know whose land was whose and which families had a claim in the tribe of the promise. Tiria is a name in that proof of title and nothing more; no act, no dwelling, no son is recorded of him. The chapter around him is full of such men, and a few of them get a sentence of narrative — Jabez his prayer, Caleb his inheritance — while the rest stand in the column. The Chronicler's purpose governs the whole: Judah was the tribe of the sceptre, and the line had to be shown unbroken from Judah to David and past David to the men then living. Tiria belongs to that demonstration. Scripture troubles itself to preserve the name of a man of whom nothing else survives, because the tribe he stood in was the tribe out of which Christ came: “For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda” (Hebrews 7:14).

corruption_summary: The Chronicler's registers are read as priestly invention; they are a returned remnant's documentation of title in the tribe from which Christ came.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatment of 1 and 2 Chronicles has long cast the genealogies as a post-exilic construction serving the interests of the temple establishment. The books present themselves otherwise, and the use the lists are put to is plain on the face of them: a people returning to a land after seventy years needed to establish who belonged to which family and which family held which portion. The registers are legal in character. That is why they include men like Tiria of whom nothing else is said — an invented list supplies stories, and a surveyed list supplies names.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the genealogies of Judah are Christological before they are tribal. Jacob's blessing had fixed the sceptre in Judah, and the Chronicler is tracing the tribe that would produce the King. Every obscure name in 1 Chronicles 4 is part of the kept record of the line, and the keeping of it was the LORD's work through men who thought they were only counting households.

pos: n. (a son of Coz in the genealogy of Judah, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Tsobebah, the slow-moving, or a walking; taken by some as a canopy or a tent; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:8.
biblical_def: Zobebah is named in a single clause of the Judahite genealogy: “And Coz begat Anub, and Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum” (1 Chronicles 4:8). The verse sits immediately before the one piece of narrative the Chronicler allows himself in this stretch of names — the prayer of Jabez, which follows two verses later. Zobebah is therefore one of the men standing in the column right beside the chapter's best-known sentence, and he gets none of its attention. He has no recorded deed, no descendant traced, and no place assigned. He is a son of Coz, and the register moves on. The Chronicler is working through the sons of Judah by household, and the households are what the post-exilic community needed: a documented claim to a portion in the tribe of the sceptre. Within that purpose the obscure name carries the same weight as the famous one. Jabez prayed and was answered and is quoted; Zobebah is listed and is silent. Both are in the book, and the book was kept by the providence of God for the generations after them, who would read it to learn whose the land was and whose the promise was.

corruption_summary: The prayer of Jabez is lifted out of its register and sold as a formula for increase; the names around it show it is a plea inside a record of ordinary households.
corruption_paragraphs: Jabez's prayer has been marketed in the modern church as a technique for enlarging one's own borders, which inverts it. In the text the prayer is an interruption in a list of men like Zobebah — a Judahite who prayed against the sorrow his own name carried and was heard by the God of Israel, in the middle of a chapter that is otherwise a property record. The setting is the correction. Jabez asked for the blessing of the covenant God on a man of the covenant people in the land of the covenant promise, and the request was granted on those terms.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prayer belongs in the ordinary register of life. The chapter does not single Jabez out as a spiritual athlete; it records that among the sons of Coz and Harum and Aharhel there was a man who called on the God of Israel. Zobebah stands next to him, unrecorded in that respect, and nothing in the text suggests the difference lay in a formula.

pos: n. (a town or clan of Judah in the house of Caleb, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Makbenah, a bond, a knot, or a cloak; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:49.
biblical_def: Machbenah appears in the Calebite section of the Judahite genealogy: “She bare also Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah, and the father of Gibea: and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah” (1 Chronicles 2:49). The Chronicler is using the idiom in which a man is called the father of a place, meaning that the family he headed founded or held the town. Machbenah is such a settlement, held by the house of Sheva in the Calebite country of southern Judah, in the neighbourhood of Madmannah. The register is working toward the land grant made to Caleb for his faithfulness at Kadesh, where he and Joshua alone brought back a true report: “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went” (Numbers 14:24). Caleb's portion is what this part of the list documents, down to the villages. Machbenah is named once and then disappears from Scripture; its site is not identified. What the verse preserves is the arrangement of a promise kept — the towns a faithful man's descendants held in the hill country, forty-five years after he asked for the mountain.

These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah; Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim,
But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it.
Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite unto this day, because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel.
corruption_summary: The conquest allotments are read as a land-grab narrative; the Calebite register documents a specific promise made to a named man and kept forty-five years later.
corruption_paragraphs: The settlement of Canaan is commonly presented now as colonial displacement dressed in religion. The texts themselves are more particular than that, and the Calebite lists are a good example. Caleb received his portion by a promise made at Kadesh-barnea, when ten spies brought an unbelieving report and two did not, and the promise named him: he would enter the land he had walked. Joshua 14 records the claim being made and honoured in old age. Machbenah is one of the villages inside that grant. The register is a record of a word kept, listed village by village.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's promises land in particular places. Caleb did not receive a sentiment; he received Hebron and the hill country, and his family held towns in it whose names Scripture still carries. The LORD who gives an inheritance to the faithful gives it with boundaries, and the obscurity of Machbenah today does not touch the fidelity recorded in naming it.

pos: n. (son of Chelub and father of Eshton, in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Mechir, a price, hire, or wages, from machar, to sell or to traffick; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:11.
biblical_def: Mehir occupies the middle place in a chain of three names: “And Chelub the brother of Shuah begat Mehir, which was the father of Eshton” (1 Chronicles 4:11). He is a son and a father, and the verse tells nothing else of him. His name is the ordinary Hebrew word for a price or wages — the term used when the prophet describes a purchase, as in “come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). A man in Judah was called Price, and the Chronicler kept the name in his register of the tribe. The chapter continues to his son's household and on through the families of the south country, each link in the chain serving the same end: the documented descent of the tribe of Judah, from which the Messiah would come. There is no narrative attached to Mehir, no land assigned to him by name, and no act recorded. He is one of the men whose whole contribution to Scripture is that he stood between his father and his son and the line did not break at him. In a book whose argument is the unbroken descent of the promise, that is not a small thing.

Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
corruption_summary: Redemption is spoken of as though it cost nothing; the word that names this man is the word Scripture uses for the price that was actually paid.
corruption_paragraphs: Cheap grace is the standing corruption here, and it has a modern dialect: forgiveness presented as God's general disposition rather than as a purchase. The Authorized Version does not speak that way. “For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's” (1 Corinthians 6:20) uses the plain commercial term, and so does Isaiah when he offers wine and milk without money and without price — free to the buyer because paid by Another. A man named Mehir, Price, stands in the genealogy of the tribe out of which the Redeemer came.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the atonement was a definite purchase of definite persons. Christ did not make redemption generally available; He redeemed His people, and the price was His blood. The Reformed doctrine of particular redemption is simply the refusal to separate the payment from the thing bought.

pos: n. (a Simeonite, father of Jehu, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Yoshibyah, the LORD will cause to dwell, or Jehovah will set in place, from yashab, to sit or to dwell, with Yah; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:35.
biblical_def: Josibiah is named once, in the Simeonite register: “And Joel, and Jehu the son of Josibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel” (1 Chronicles 4:35). He is a link in a four-deep descent, and the list he stands in is one of the few places Scripture follows the tribe of Simeon after the conquest. The passage goes on to record that these men sought room for their flocks and found it: the Simeonite princes took the valley of Gedor and smote the Meunim, and dwelt there. His name is a confession — Jehovah will cause to dwell — and it is attached to a man in the one genealogy in Chronicles that ends with a tribe actually finding a place to dwell. Simeon's portion had been swallowed inside Judah's, and the tribe was under Jacob's word of scattering: “I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). Yet the LORD gave these households pasture. Josibiah himself does nothing in the record; his son and his son's companions do. He is a name that states what God does, carried by a man of a scattered tribe whose family the LORD settled.

corruption_summary: Jacob's word of scattering upon Simeon is read as a curse God never relented from; Chronicles shows the LORD giving the scattered households pasture.
corruption_paragraphs: Simeon is the tribe modern readers forget, and the reason is in Genesis 49, where Jacob divides and scatters Simeon and Levi for the slaughter at Shechem. The lesson drawn is often fatalistic: a tribe written off. Chronicles complicates that reading without contradicting it. The word stood — Simeon never held an undivided territory, and its towns lay inside Judah's border — and yet the LORD gave these particular families increase, and room, and a victory, and the Chronicler recorded their names.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's chastisements are not His abandonment. Levi, scattered under the same word, was scattered into the priesthood and given the LORD Himself for an inheritance. A man named Jehovah-will-cause-to-dwell, standing in Simeon's short register, is a small witness that the God who divides a tribe can still settle a household.
